title: Maternal Smoking in Pregnancy and Birth Defects: Epidemiology, Mechanisms, Evidence Synthesis, and Public Health Implications

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Scope of the Research Field
subsections.content:
In studies of congenital anomalies, maternal smoking exposure is typically defined along three dimensions: timing, intensity, and source. Timing is especially important because organogenesis is concentrated in the periconceptional period and first trimester, so exposure windows may be specified as smoking before conception, during the month before pregnancy, in early pregnancy, or across the entire gestation. Many epidemiologic studies therefore distinguish any smoking from trimester-specific smoking and from persistent versus discontinued smoking, recognizing that quitting after pregnancy recognition may not eliminate exposure during critical developmental windows ref [1], ref [2].

Exposure ascertainment has most often relied on maternal self-report, usually recorded on birth certificates, prenatal interviews, or postpartum questionnaires. Self-reported measures can classify women as never, former, occasional, or current smokers and may further quantify cigarettes per day to capture dose-response patterns. However, self-report is vulnerable to under-ascertainment because smoking during pregnancy is socially stigmatized; biochemical validation using cotinine in serum, urine, or saliva has repeatedly shown misclassification of active smoking status in pregnant populations ref [3], ref [4].

A comprehensive definition of maternal smoking exposure also extends beyond active combustible cigarette use. It may include environmental tobacco smoke (passive smoking), use of other nicotine-containing products, and cumulative fetal exposure inferred from biomarkers. For etiologic syntheses, clear operational definitions are therefore essential: they determine comparability across studies, influence estimates of teratogenic risk, and shape interpretation of whether observed associations reflect active smoking itself, correlated behaviors, or broader tobacco-smoke exposure ref [4], ref [5].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Scope of the Research Field
subsections.content:
Birth defects are commonly classified along several complementary axes that are important for epidemiologic studies of maternal smoking. A basic distinction separates major structural anomalies, which have medical, surgical, or cosmetic significance, from minor anomalies, which are more limited in clinical consequence. Surveillance systems also distinguish congenital malformations from chromosomal disorders, single-gene conditions, and functional or developmental disorders, because these groups differ in etiology, detectability, and plausibility of association with exogenous prenatal exposures ref [6], ref [7].

For analytic purposes, structural defects are usually organized by organ system, including neural tube defects, orofacial clefts, congenital heart defects, musculoskeletal anomalies, gastrointestinal defects, genitourinary anomalies, and limb reduction defects. International classification frameworks such as the ICD and CDC/British Pediatric Association coding systems enable standardized case ascertainment across registries and studies, while EUROCAT further promotes harmonized subgroup definitions and exclusions for multiple congenital anomaly patterns ref [8], ref [9]. This granularity is essential because smoking-related risks are unlikely to be uniform across heterogeneous defect groupings.

A further conceptual distinction concerns isolated defects, multiple congenital anomalies, and syndromic presentations. Isolated defects are often preferred in teratogenic research because they reduce etiologic heterogeneity, whereas syndromic or chromosomal cases may reflect mechanisms less directly related to maternal smoking exposure. Modern surveillance practice therefore emphasizes careful phenotyping, timing of diagnosis, and inclusion of live births, stillbirths, and where possible prenatally diagnosed terminations, all of which affect prevalence estimates and comparability across studies ref [7], ref [9], ref [10].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Scope of the Research Field
subsections.content:
Congenital anomalies constitute a major component of perinatal and child morbidity and mortality worldwide. Population-based estimates indicate that serious birth defects affect a substantial minority of births and contribute disproportionately to fetal loss, neonatal death, long-term disability, repeated hospitalization, and specialized health-care use ref [11], ref [12]. Because many affected children now survive into adolescence and adulthood, the burden is not limited to the perinatal period but extends across the life course, with implications for neurodevelopment, functional status, education, and family well-being ref [12], ref [13].

The burden is also heterogeneous across anomaly groups. Structural malformations such as congenital heart defects, orofacial clefts, neural tube defects, limb reduction defects, and gastrointestinal malformations differ in prevalence, severity, detectability, and survival, so aggregate measures can obscure clinically important variation ref [13], ref [14]. From an epidemiologic perspective, this heterogeneity is central when evaluating maternal smoking during pregnancy, because even modest relative risks can translate into meaningful population-attributable burden for common defects, whereas rarer but severe defects may generate substantial individual and health-system impact.

Importantly, the observed burden of congenital anomalies reflects not only biological occurrence but also access to prenatal screening, termination policies, diagnostic coding, and registry completeness. International surveillance programs have shown that prevalence estimates vary by case ascertainment strategy and whether live births, stillbirths, and terminations of pregnancy for fetal anomaly are all included ref [14], ref [15]. These measurement issues are especially relevant for evidence synthesis on smoking-related teratogenicity, since they affect comparability across studies and the interpretation of preventable risk.

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Scope of the Research Field
subsections.subsection_title: Maternal smoking as a modifiable prenatal exposure
subsections.content:
Maternal smoking during pregnancy is a paradigmatic modifiable prenatal exposure because it is behaviorally mediated, measurable across the preconception-to-delivery period, and amenable to clinical and public-health intervention. In perinatal epidemiology, its importance derives not only from its prevalence but also from the biologic plausibility of fetal harm: tobacco smoke delivers nicotine, carbon monoxide, and numerous oxidants and toxicants that can impair placental perfusion, reduce oxygen delivery, and perturb embryonic development during critical windows of organogenesis ref [16], ref [17].

The designation "modifiable" is nevertheless nuanced. Smoking behavior is socially patterned, strongly shaped by nicotine dependence, stress, mental health, and co-exposures, so risk reduction depends on more than individual choice. Even so, cessation at or before pregnancy remains achievable and clinically meaningful, and randomized and quasi-experimental evidence supports the effectiveness of structured cessation support, particularly behavioral counseling and incentive-based approaches, for increasing abstinence in pregnancy ref [18], ref [19]. From a prevention perspective, this makes smoking distinct from many fixed teratogenic risk factors: exposure can in principle be reduced in dose, duration, or timing.

For studies of congenital anomalies, treating smoking as modifiable also has analytic implications. It motivates attention to dose-response, timing of cessation relative to the first trimester, and the possibility that observed associations reflect preventable risk rather than immutable susceptibility. At the population level, reductions in prenatal smoking have been linked to improvements in adverse birth outcomes, reinforcing the public-health relevance of smoking control before and during pregnancy ref [20].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Foundations and Scope of the Research Field
subsections.subsection_title: Historical development of research on smoking and congenital anomalies
subsections.content:
Research on maternal smoking and congenital anomalies emerged alongside the broader epidemiologic recognition of smoking as an adverse pregnancy exposure. Early work focused primarily on fetal growth restriction, preterm birth, and perinatal mortality, but by the late twentieth century investigators began testing whether cigarette smoke might also act as a teratogen. A major conceptual shift occurred when large population-based case-control surveillance systems made it possible to study relatively rare structural defects with sufficient statistical power and standardized phenotyping, moving the field beyond small hospital series and inconsistent anomaly groupings ref [21], ref [22].

By the 1990s and early 2000s, studies increasingly examined specific defect phenotypes rather than congenital anomalies as a single outcome. This period produced some of the most reproducible associations, particularly for orofacial clefts and certain limb reduction defects. For example, meta-analytic synthesis reported elevated risks of oral clefts among offspring of mothers who smoked during pregnancy, while analyses from the National Birth Defects Prevention Study strengthened evidence for selected defect-specific associations and highlighted substantial heterogeneity across malformations ref [23], ref [24]. These developments encouraged more careful attention to critical exposure windows, dose-response patterns, and confounding by correlated maternal behaviors.

More recent research has been shaped by evidence synthesis and causal inference concerns. Comprehensive reviews have concluded that the literature supports associations for a limited subset of anomalies rather than a uniform teratogenic effect across all defect classes ref [25]. At the same time, methodologic debates have centered on exposure misclassification from self-reported smoking, residual confounding by socioeconomic and nutritional factors, and the challenge of separating direct toxic effects from shared familial or behavioral risks. The historical trajectory of the field has therefore been one of increasing phenotypic resolution, larger collaborative datasets, and more cautious interpretation of defect-specific risk estimates ref [22], ref [25], ref [26].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiologic Evidence on the Association Between Maternal Smoking and Specific Birth Defects
subsections.content:
At the broadest level, epidemiologic studies assessing maternal smoking in relation to any congenital anomaly have generally suggested at most a modest elevation in overall risk, with substantial heterogeneity masked by composite outcomes. Early syntheses already noted that pooling all malformations together can dilute associations because smoking appears more strongly related to some phenotypes than to others ref [27]. Consequently, summary estimates for “any birth defect” should be interpreted cautiously, as they reflect a mixture of null, weakly positive, and occasionally inverse associations across disparate developmental pathways.

Large registry-based and population-based studies have often reported small increases in the prevalence of any major congenital anomaly among infants of smokers, but the magnitude is typically less pronounced than for selected defect groups such as orofacial clefts or gastroschisis ref [28], ref [29]. Meta-analytic evidence likewise indicates that the overall excess risk is limited, while reinforcing that phenotype-specific analyses are more informative than aggregate categories ref [30]. This pattern is epidemiologically plausible: tobacco smoke contains multiple toxicants with teratogenic potential, yet susceptibility likely depends on timing, dose, genetic background, and the embryologic process involved.

Interpretation of the overall literature is further complicated by exposure misclassification, residual confounding by socioeconomic and behavioral factors, and differences in case ascertainment, especially regarding elective terminations and minor anomalies. More recent analyses using linked administrative or surveillance data continue to support the view that maternal smoking is not uniformly associated with all congenital anomalies, but instead contributes to risk in a selective manner best captured through defect-specific investigation ref [31].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiologic Evidence on the Association Between Maternal Smoking and Specific Birth Defects
subsections.content:
Craniofacial defects provide some of the strongest and most consistently replicated signals in the literature on maternal smoking and birth defects. The association is most robust for oral clefts, particularly cleft lip with or without cleft palate, whereas evidence for isolated cleft palate is generally weaker and more heterogeneous. A meta-analysis of observational studies reported elevated risks for both cleft lip with or without cleft palate and cleft palate among infants of mothers who smoked during pregnancy, supporting a phenotype-specific effect rather than a uniform increase across all craniofacial anomalies [1].

Large population-based studies and pooled analyses have helped refine this pattern. Analysis from the U.S. National Birth Defects Prevention Study found maternal smoking to be associated with several cleft phenotypes, with stronger effects for cleft lip-related defects than for cleft palate alone [2]. Similarly, an international pooled analysis from the International Clearinghouse for Birth Defects Surveillance and Research reported increased risks of oral clefts with maternal cigarette smoking, reinforcing the consistency of the signal across settings [3].

Interpretation remains influenced by exposure misclassification, residual confounding, and the possibility that smoking interacts with genetic susceptibility. Gene-environment studies have suggested that variants involved in detoxification and craniofacial development may modify smoking-related cleft risk, although replication has been incomplete [4]. Overall, the epidemiologic evidence supports maternal smoking as a modest but credible risk factor for selected craniofacial defects, especially cleft lip with or without cleft palate, underscoring the importance of analyzing craniofacial phenotypes separately rather than as a single anomaly group [1,5].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiologic Evidence on the Association Between Maternal Smoking and Specific Birth Defects
subsections.content:
Cardiovascular malformations are among the most intensively studied outcomes in relation to maternal smoking because they are common, etiologically heterogeneous, and often detectable in population-based registries. The epidemiologic literature generally does not support a strong elevation in risk for all congenital heart defects combined, but instead suggests modest, phenotype-specific associations. In a population-based analysis from the National Birth Defects Prevention Study, maternal smoking was associated more consistently with septal and right-sided obstructive lesions than with conotruncal defects overall ref [37]. Similar heterogeneity was emphasized in a meta-analysis that found only small increases in risk for congenital heart defects overall, with stronger signals for selected subtypes rather than a uniform effect across all cardiac phenotypes ref [38].

Evidence is most consistent for septal defects, particularly atrial septal defects, and for some outflow or right ventricular obstruction phenotypes. An analysis of Swedish registry data reported elevated risks for heart septal defects among infants of smoking mothers, supporting the view that smoking-related susceptibility may be concentrated in defects arising from specific developmental pathways ref [39]. More recent pooled evidence has also identified associations with pulmonary valve and pulmonary artery anomalies, although effect sizes remain modest and confidence intervals vary across studies ref [38].

Interpretation remains complicated by exposure misclassification, residual confounding by socioeconomic and behavioral factors, and phenotype misclassification when studies aggregate dissimilar lesions. Nonetheless, the pattern across large surveillance systems and meta-analyses suggests that maternal smoking is better understood as a weak to moderate risk factor for selected cardiac subtypes rather than a major determinant of congenital heart defects as a whole ref [37], ref [38], ref [40].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiologic Evidence on the Association Between Maternal Smoking and Specific Birth Defects
subsections.subsection_title: Neural tube and central nervous system defects
subsections.content:
Evidence linking maternal smoking with neural tube defects (NTDs) and other central nervous system malformations is less consistent than for some craniofacial phenotypes. Large population-based analyses and meta-analytic syntheses generally report weak or null overall associations for NTDs, with substantial heterogeneity by study design, exposure ascertainment, and adjustment for folate-related and socioeconomic confounding ref [41], ref [42]. This pattern has encouraged cautious interpretation of modest elevations in risk, particularly because smoking is strongly correlated with maternal nutrition, alcohol use, and other factors that may independently influence neurulation.

Systematic review evidence suggests that any excess risk is small and may be phenotype-specific rather than uniform across spina bifida, anencephaly, and encephalocele ref [41], ref [43]. Case-control studies have reported elevated odds for selected CNS outcomes in some settings, but these findings are not always replicated in registry-based cohorts ref [42], ref [44]. The biologic plausibility of an effect remains credible, given smoking-related fetal hypoxia, oxidative stress, and interference with one-carbon metabolism, yet the epidemiologic signal is attenuated compared with defects more consistently associated with maternal smoking.

An additional complication is that smoking may differentially affect survival to ascertainment. For severe CNS malformations, variation in prenatal diagnosis and termination practices can distort observed birth-prevalence associations if studies are limited to live births. Accordingly, the literature supports a nuanced conclusion: maternal smoking is not a strong or uniformly demonstrated risk factor for NTDs overall, but modest associations for particular CNS phenotypes cannot be excluded and warrant phenotype-specific analysis in datasets with complete ascertainment ref [43], ref [45].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiologic Evidence on the Association Between Maternal Smoking and Specific Birth Defects
subsections.content:
Evidence for gastrointestinal and abdominal wall defects suggests stronger and more phenotype-specific associations with maternal smoking than are seen for many other anomaly groups. The clearest signal is for gastroschisis, a defect that has repeatedly shown elevated risk among infants of smokers, often with indications of dose-response and possible interaction with young maternal age. Population-based case-control analyses from the United States and Europe have consistently reported increased odds of gastroschisis among mothers who smoked in early pregnancy, supporting a relationship that is unlikely to be explained entirely by socioeconomic confounding ref [46], ref [47].

By contrast, findings for other gastrointestinal malformations are more heterogeneous. In the large National Birth Defects Prevention Study analysis by Honein and colleagues, maternal smoking was associated with selected defects, including gastroschisis, but not uniformly across digestive tract phenotypes ref [48]. Reviews of smoking and birth defects similarly conclude that abdominal wall defects, especially gastroschisis, show one of the more consistent positive associations, whereas evidence for anomalies such as esophageal atresia, anorectal malformations, or intestinal atresias is less robust and often based on smaller numbers ref [41].

Mechanistically, the predominance of gastroschisis in this literature is biologically plausible because smoking may contribute to vascular disruption, oxidative stress, or impaired embryonic body-wall development. Nonetheless, residual confounding by maternal age, nutrition, and correlated substance use remains a concern. Overall, the epidemiologic literature supports abdominal wall defects—and particularly gastroschisis—as a key phenotype in which maternal smoking appears most consistently implicated, while the broader category of gastrointestinal malformations shows weaker and less reproducible associations ref [46], ref [48], ref [49].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiologic Evidence on the Association Between Maternal Smoking and Specific Birth Defects
subsections.content:
Evidence on musculoskeletal and limb anomalies suggests that any association with maternal smoking is more phenotype-specific than global. Large population-based analyses and meta-analytic syntheses generally do not support a strong elevation in all musculoskeletal defects combined, but they do indicate modestly increased risks for selected limb-reduction phenotypes and for clubfoot (talipes equinovarus) [1,2]. This heterogeneity is consistent with the broader congenital-anomaly literature, in which aggregation across anatomically diverse outcomes can obscure narrower associations.

Clubfoot is the best studied musculoskeletal outcome in this context. A meta-analysis by Honein et al. reported an increased risk of clubfoot among infants of mothers who smoked during pregnancy [3], and subsequent epidemiologic studies have reinforced this signal, including work suggesting that smoking may act jointly with familial susceptibility or developmental pathway variants rather than as a uniformly strong independent teratogen [4]. The magnitude of association is typically modest, but the consistency of findings across designs has made clubfoot one of the more credible smoking-related musculoskeletal phenotypes.

For limb-reduction defects, evidence is suggestive but less uniform. In the National Birth Defects Prevention Study, maternal cigarette smoking was associated with selected congenital limb deficiencies, with stronger findings for some transverse and longitudinal reduction subtypes than others [5]. More broadly, the meta-analysis by Hackshaw et al. found increased risks for musculoskeletal defects overall, though interpretation is limited by between-study heterogeneity and variable case definitions [2]. Overall, the literature supports phenotype-specific analysis within the musculoskeletal category, with the clearest concerns centered on clubfoot and some limb-reduction defects rather than a generalized increase in all limb anomalies.

subsections.section_title: Epidemiologic Evidence on the Association Between Maternal Smoking and Specific Birth Defects
subsections.content:
Evidence for genitourinary and reproductive defects suggests a more phenotype-specific association with maternal smoking than a uniform increase across all anomalies. The clearest and most replicated signal concerns cryptorchidism: epidemiologic studies and pooled analyses generally report a modest elevation in risk among sons of women who smoked during pregnancy, although effect sizes vary and residual confounding by correlated social and reproductive factors remains a concern ref [55], ref [56]. A similar pattern has been described for hypospadias, but findings are less consistent, with some studies reporting weak positive associations and others observing little association after adjustment for maternal characteristics ref [57], ref [58].

Interpretation is complicated by etiologic heterogeneity within the genitourinary category. Male genital anomalies such as cryptorchidism and hypospadias have been hypothesized to reflect disrupted endocrine signaling during fetal development, providing biological plausibility for an effect of tobacco smoke constituents. However, registry-based studies indicate that any smoking-related increase is small relative to the contributions of prematurity, fetal growth restriction, and other maternal exposures that cluster with smoking ref [55], ref [57]. Moreover, broad groupings of renal and urinary tract malformations have not shown a comparably consistent smoking signal in the literature, underscoring the need to disaggregate upper urinary tract, obstructive, and external genital phenotypes in future analyses.

Overall, the epidemiologic literature supports at most modest associations between maternal smoking and selected reproductive anomalies, particularly cryptorchidism, while evidence for hypospadias and other genitourinary defects remains mixed. This pattern reinforces a central theme of the birth-defects literature: smoking effects, if present, are unlikely to be homogeneous across organ systems and are best evaluated using narrowly defined phenotypes and careful control of confounding ref [56], ref [58], ref [59].

subsections.section_title: Epidemiologic Evidence on the Association Between Maternal Smoking and Specific Birth Defects
subsections.content:
A recurring issue in this literature is that the apparent association between maternal smoking and congenital anomalies depends strongly on whether analyses aggregate heterogeneous phenotypes or isolate specific, relatively rare defects. Large meta-analyses and registry-based studies have shown that overall congenital anomaly risk is only modestly elevated, if at all, whereas clearer signals emerge for selected phenotypes such as orofacial clefts, gastroschisis, and some limb-reduction defects; combining these with more common but etiologically distinct anomalies can dilute subtype-specific effects and obscure biologic heterogeneity ref [60], ref [41].

This problem is especially important for rare defects, where small numbers reduce precision but finer phenotypic classification may reveal stronger associations. For example, analyses of birth-defects surveillance data have reported phenotype-specific elevations for gastroschisis in relation to periconceptional smoking, while broader abdominal wall defect groupings may mask differences between gastroschisis and omphalocele ref [61]. Similarly, studies of multiple congenital anomaly groupings emphasize that epidemiologic inference is sensitive to whether investigators analyze isolated defects, syndromic presentations, or broad organ-system categories ref [62].

Accordingly, interpretation of smoking teratogenicity benefits from a hierarchical approach: broad analyses are useful for estimating public-health burden, but rare-defect studies often provide sharper etiologic insight. The strongest evidence to date suggests that maternal smoking is not uniformly associated across all defect phenotypes; rather, risk concentrates in a limited set of specific, sometimes uncommon anomalies, underscoring the need for standardized subphenotype definitions, pooled consortia, and sufficiently powered registry linkages ref [60], ref [41], ref [63].

subsections.section_title: Biological and Developmental Mechanisms Underlying Teratogenic Risk
subsections.subsection_title: Tobacco smoke constituents and fetal toxicity
subsections.content:
Tobacco smoke is a complex aerosol containing thousands of chemicals, but several constituents are especially relevant to fetal toxicity. Nicotine readily crosses the placenta and accumulates in fetal compartments, where it can activate nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the developing nervous system and vasculature, altering cell proliferation, differentiation, and autonomic regulation ref [64], ref [65]. Carbon monoxide further compounds risk by forming carboxyhemoglobin and reducing oxygen delivery to embryonic and fetal tissues, while polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, tobacco-specific nitrosamines, and heavy metals such as cadmium contribute direct toxicant burden.

These constituents reach the conceptus despite placental filtering. Experimental and human studies indicate that benzo[a]pyrene and related polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons can form bulky DNA adducts in placental and fetal tissues, providing a plausible route from maternal exposure to mutagenic and dysmorphogenic effects ref [66]. Cadmium is also of particular interest because it accumulates in placenta, perturbs transporter function, and may interfere with nutrient transfer and endocrine signaling, thereby linking chemical exposure to growth restriction ref [67].

At a mechanistic level, the toxicologic profile of cigarette smoke is therefore not reducible to a single agent. Rather, combined exposure to nicotine, combustion gases, carcinogenic hydrocarbons, and metals likely produces additive or synergistic effects on rapidly developing organs, helping explain why prenatal smoking has been associated with impaired fetal growth, congenital anomalies in some organ systems, and later-life cardiopulmonary and neurobehavioral vulnerability ref [65], ref [68].

subsections.section_title: Biological and Developmental Mechanisms Underlying Teratogenic Risk
subsections.content:
The placenta is a central mediator of tobacco-related developmental toxicity because it regulates maternal-fetal gas exchange, nutrient transfer, and endocrine signaling. Maternal smoking has consistently been associated with structural and functional placental abnormalities, including increased placental weight relative to birthweight, impaired trophoblast differentiation, and lesions consistent with maternal vascular underperfusion, all of which can reduce effective exchange capacity and constrain fetal growth ref [69], ref [70]. These placental changes provide a mechanistic bridge between prenatal smoke exposure and outcomes such as fetal growth restriction, preterm birth, and stillbirth.

A key pathway is chronic fetal hypoxia. Carbon monoxide in tobacco smoke forms carboxyhemoglobin and diminishes oxygen delivery, while nicotine promotes vasoconstriction in uteroplacental vessels, together lowering oxygen availability at the maternal-fetal interface. Experimental work has shown that nicotine can directly reduce uterine blood flow, supporting a hemodynamic mechanism for placental insufficiency ref [71]. Human placental studies further indicate altered angiogenic signaling and vascular development in smoking-exposed pregnancies, including dysregulation of placental growth factor pathways that are critical for villous vascularization ref [72].

These disturbances are biologically plausible contributors to asymmetric fetal growth and organ vulnerability because prolonged mild hypoxemia can redistribute fetal circulation toward the brain and heart at the expense of somatic growth. Consistent with this framework, reviews of smoking in pregnancy emphasize convergent toxic, vascular, and hypoxic mechanisms rather than a single causal agent ref [73]. Thus, placental dysfunction and fetal hypoxia likely represent intertwined processes through which tobacco smoke exposure translates maternal inhalational exposure into altered fetal development.

subsections.section_title: Biological and Developmental Mechanisms Underlying Teratogenic Risk
subsections.content:
Oxidative stress is a plausible intermediary linking maternal smoking to teratogenic injury because cigarette smoke contains abundant free radicals and reactive aldehydes that can overwhelm embryonic and placental antioxidant defenses. Early conceptuses are especially vulnerable: organogenesis occurs under relatively low-oxygen conditions, and immature antioxidant enzyme systems limit the capacity to neutralize reactive oxygen species. Experimental work has shown that nicotine and other smoke-related toxicants can increase lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and apoptotic signaling in placental and fetal tissues, thereby providing a mechanistic bridge between exposure and structural or growth-related abnormalities ref [74], ref [75].

In the placenta, oxidative injury may amplify other pathogenic pathways by damaging syncytiotrophoblast membranes, reducing nitric oxide bioavailability, and promoting inflammatory and antiangiogenic responses. Such changes can impair nutrient transport and uteroplacental perfusion, further increasing hypoxia-reoxygenation stress and cellular injury. Reviews of placental oxidative stress in complicated pregnancy have emphasized that excessive reactive oxygen species can trigger DNA damage, protein oxidation, and trophoblast apoptosis, all of which are biologically compatible with smoking-associated fetal growth restriction and congenital maldevelopment ref [76], ref [77].

A related concern is oxidative damage to nucleic acids. Tobacco exposure has been associated with elevated biomarkers of oxidatively modified DNA, including 8-hydroxydeoxyguanosine, in maternal and cord compartments, suggesting that genotoxic stress reaches the developing fetus. Persistent oxidative DNA lesions during critical developmental windows could interfere with cell-cycle regulation, differentiation, and tissue morphogenesis, helping to explain why even modest smoking exposure may have disproportionate effects early in gestation ref [78].

subsections.section_title: Biological and Developmental Mechanisms Underlying Teratogenic Risk
subsections.content:
Gene–environment interaction frameworks are especially relevant to prenatal tobacco exposure because the fetal dose and biologic consequences of smoke constituents depend partly on maternal and fetal variation in xenobiotic metabolism, DNA damage responses, and vascular regulation. Candidate-gene studies have most consistently focused on enzymes involved in phase I and phase II detoxification, particularly CYP1A1 and GSTT1/GSTM1, where susceptibility may arise from greater bioactivation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons or diminished conjugation capacity. In a prospective birth cohort, Wang and colleagues reported stronger adverse effects of prenatal polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon exposure on birth outcomes among infants carrying a CYP1A1 variant together with GSTT1 null genotype, illustrating how inherited differences can amplify toxic effects relevant to tobacco smoke exposure ref [79].

Evidence from congenital anomaly research also suggests that maternal smoking may interact with genes involved in developmental signaling and folate-related pathways. In case-parent analyses of oral clefts, variants in transforming growth factor pathways showed interaction with maternal smoking, supporting the view that smoke exposure perturbs morphogenetic programs in genetically susceptible embryos ref [80]. More broadly, a large review of gene–environment studies in cleft lip and palate identified recurrent signals for interactions between maternal smoking and loci in detoxification and craniofacial development pathways, while emphasizing modest effect sizes and problems of replication ref [81].

These findings support a multifactorial model in which tobacco-related teratogenicity is conditional rather than uniform across pregnancies. However, most reported interactions come from small candidate-gene studies vulnerable to population stratification and multiple-testing bias. The field has therefore shifted toward genome-wide interaction approaches and better-powered consortia, as exemplified by genome-wide studies of maternal smoking and birth weight that attempt to move beyond a priori candidate pathways ref [82]. Integrating fetal and maternal genotypes with exposure biomarkers and placental molecular phenotypes will be essential for clarifying which interactions are biologically meaningful rather than statistically incidental.

subsections.section_title: Biological and Developmental Mechanisms Underlying Teratogenic Risk
subsections.content:
Prenatal tobacco smoke exposure is increasingly interpreted through a developmental programming framework in which early environmental insults leave durable epigenetic marks that alter gene regulation without changing DNA sequence. Human epigenome-wide studies have shown reproducible differences in neonatal cord blood DNA methylation associated with maternal smoking, particularly at loci involved in xenobiotic metabolism and growth regulation, including AHRR, CYP1A1, and GFI1, supporting the view that cigarette smoke can become biologically embedded during gestation ref [83], ref [84]. These signatures are notable because several persist beyond birth, suggesting that in utero exposure may reshape regulatory trajectories rather than induce only transient fetal stress responses ref [85].

Mechanistically, tobacco smoke contains nicotine, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, heavy metals, and oxidants that can perturb one-carbon metabolism, transcription factor binding, and chromatin remodeling, thereby influencing DNA methylation and other epigenetic processes. Placental tissues also exhibit smoking-related methylation changes, including at genes linked to detoxification and placental function, indicating that epigenetic disruption may occur at the maternal-fetal interface as well as in fetal compartments ref [86]. Such alterations provide a plausible bridge between exposure and downstream phenotypes, including impaired growth, altered neurobehavioral development, and later cardiometabolic vulnerability.

Although causality remains difficult to establish, the consistency of smoking-associated methylation signals across cohorts, together with evidence that some marks are detectable into childhood, strengthens the hypothesis that epigenetic dysregulation is one mediator of teratogenic risk rather than merely a biomarker of exposure ref [84], ref [87]. An important implication is that susceptibility may depend on timing, dose, and fetal genotype, with early embryogenesis and placental development representing particularly sensitive windows in which epigenetic perturbation could have lasting developmental consequences.

subsections.section_title: Biological and Developmental Mechanisms Underlying Teratogenic Risk
subsections.content:
Teratogenic risk from maternal smoking is strongly time-dependent because embryonic structures are most vulnerable during brief windows of rapid proliferation, migration, and morphogenesis. Experimental embryology established that susceptibility varies by developmental stage rather than exposure alone, with organ-specific effects emerging when toxic insult coincides with the period of tissue determination and fusion ref [88]. This principle is especially relevant to tobacco smoke, whose constituents can simultaneously perturb oxygen delivery, redox balance, and signaling pathways that guide early patterning.

For structural malformations, the first trimester is likely the most critical interval. Craniofacial development is highly stage-specific: disruption of neural crest cell survival or palatal shelf growth during early facial morphogenesis can produce clefts, and epidemiologic evidence has linked periconceptional and early-pregnancy maternal smoking to elevated risks of oral clefts ref [23], ref [89]. Cardiac morphogenesis may be similarly sensitive, because looping, septation, and outflow tract formation occur early in gestation; correspondingly, reviews of congenital heart defect epidemiology identify maternal smoking as a modest but recurrent risk factor, consistent with vulnerability during these narrow developmental windows ref [90].

Later gestation may be less relevant for major malformations but remains important for fetal growth, lung maturation, and neurodevelopment, suggesting that the phenotype produced by smoking may shift over time from structural anomalies to growth restriction and functional programming. This temporal framework aligns with the developmental origins paradigm, in which insults during critical periods induce lasting changes in organ structure and physiology ref [91]. Accordingly, studies that distinguish preconception, early first-trimester, and sustained smoking exposure are likely to be more informative mechanistically than analyses based only on smoking at any time during pregnancy.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Approaches in Observational Studies and Systematic Reviews
subsections.content:
Perinatal epidemiology on maternal smoking and congenital anomalies has relied predominantly on observational designs, especially population-based case-control studies and retrospective or prospective birth cohorts. Case-control designs are efficient for rare, etiologically heterogeneous outcomes such as specific malformation phenotypes, and they have underpinned much of the evidence synthesized in major reviews of maternal smoking and birth defects ref [92], ref [17]. Cohort designs, particularly those built from linked birth, hospital, and anomaly-registry data, offer clearer temporality and reduced recall error, but often require very large underlying populations to study individual defects with adequate precision.

Design choice strongly shapes internal validity. Registry-based studies improve ascertainment of both births and diagnosed anomalies, as illustrated by EUROCAT and other surveillance systems that standardize case definition and permit multi-country analyses ref [93]. However, studies restricted to live births can induce selection bias when smoking affects fetal loss or pregnancy termination following prenatal diagnosis, a longstanding concern in birth-defect epidemiology ref [94]. Inclusion of stillbirths and terminations, when available, therefore materially improves comparability across studies.

More recent quasi-experimental and family-based approaches aim to strengthen causal inference beyond conventional adjusted associations. Negative-control comparisons and sibling-comparison designs have been proposed to address shared familial and social confounding in prenatal exposure research ref [95], ref [96]. Although such designs are not yet dominant in the smoking–malformation literature, they are methodologically important because they probe whether observed associations reflect intrauterine effects, residual confounding, or selective reproductive processes.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Approaches in Observational Studies and Systematic Reviews
subsections.content:
Exposure assessment is a central source of heterogeneity in studies of maternal smoking and congenital anomalies. Most investigations rely on maternal self-report collected during prenatal care, at delivery, or retrospectively after an affected birth; these approaches differ in recall window and susceptibility to social desirability bias. Validation studies consistently show under-ascertainment of smoking during pregnancy when self-report is compared with biomarkers such as cotinine, implying nondifferential misclassification in some cohorts but potentially differential error in case-control studies if mothers of affected infants report differently from controls ref [3], ref [97]. This problem is especially important for malformations whose critical exposure window is the periconceptional period, which is not always captured by routine antenatal questionnaires.

Measurement validity also depends on how smoking is parameterized. Binary ever/never measures obscure dose-response patterns and changes across trimesters, whereas quantity, duration, quitting, passive smoke exposure, and use of nicotine products may each carry different etiologic relevance. Biochemical markers improve specificity but usually reflect recent exposure rather than cumulative intake, and they are rarely available in large administrative datasets or pooled historical studies ref [4]. Consequently, meta-analyses often combine studies with materially different exposure definitions, reducing comparability and widening between-study heterogeneity.

A further challenge is temporal and contextual variation in reporting quality. Population-level declines in smoking prevalence, stronger stigma, and increasing use of assisted reproductive technologies and prenatal screening may alter both exposure disclosure and the composition of observed case series over time. Methodologically, stronger studies define a priori exposure windows tied to embryologic development, distinguish active from passive smoking, and where possible triangulate self-report with biomarkers or repeated measurements ref [98], ref [16]. Such design features are crucial for interpreting pooled estimates and for judging whether null or modest associations reflect biology or exposure misclassification.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Approaches in Observational Studies and Systematic Reviews
subsections.content:
Outcome ascertainment is a central source of between-study heterogeneity in research on maternal smoking and congenital anomalies. Case identification may rely on birth certificates, hospital discharge files, congenital anomaly registries, or active clinical review, and these sources differ substantially in sensitivity, completeness, and diagnostic precision. Population-based surveillance programs have shown that prevalence estimates vary according to whether ascertainment includes live births only or also stillbirths and pregnancy terminations for fetal anomaly, with important implications for defects that are frequently detected prenatally and electively terminated ref [99], ref [100]. As a result, pooled estimates can mix studies capturing fundamentally different underlying case populations.

Diagnostic heterogeneity also arises from changing classification systems and phenotype definitions. Broad groupings such as “cardiovascular malformations” or “orofacial clefts” can obscure etiologic differences between isolated and multiple defects, minor and major anomalies, and embryologically distinct subtypes. EUROCAT guidance has emphasized standardized coding, exclusion of minor anomalies, and careful handling of multiple congenital anomaly cases to improve comparability across registries ref [9]. For smoking-related analyses, this matters because associations may be diluted when etiologically heterogeneous phenotypes are aggregated, or exaggerated when differential diagnostic work-up increases subtype detection in certain settings.

A further challenge is temporal improvement in prenatal imaging, neonatal echocardiography, and registry linkage, which can create secular changes in detection unrelated to exposure. Validation work in congenital anomaly surveillance shows that registry quality depends on active case finding and standardized verification procedures ref [101]. Meta-analyses should therefore prioritize harmonized case definitions, distinguish isolated from syndromic defects where possible, and consider stratification by ascertainment source and inclusion of terminations to reduce misclassification-driven inconsistency ref [102].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Approaches in Observational Studies and Systematic Reviews
subsections.subsection_title: Confounding, bias, and causal inference challenges
subsections.content:
Causal interpretation of associations between maternal smoking and congenital anomalies is constrained by strong confounding from socioeconomic position, maternal age, parity, alcohol and other substance use, nutritional status, obesity, diabetes, and co-medication patterns. In perinatal epidemiology, these factors are often imperfectly measured and may vary across pregnancy, leaving substantial residual confounding even in large registry-based studies. Directed-acyclic-graph approaches and explicit confounder selection have therefore been recommended to avoid both underadjustment and inappropriate control for intermediates or colliders ref [103].

Selection and information biases are also prominent. Restriction to live births can induce live-birth bias because smoking may affect fetal loss and termination following prenatal diagnosis, potentially distorting defect-specific estimates among surviving pregnancies ref [104]. Exposure misclassification is another persistent problem: self-reported smoking in pregnancy is affected by underreporting and differential disclosure, while dose, timing, cessation, and passive exposure are often crudely captured. Validation studies using biomarkers such as cotinine show that misclassification can be substantial, generally biasing estimates toward the null but also complicating between-study comparability ref [3].

Because conventional adjustment may not fully resolve these problems, quasi-experimental and family-based strategies have gained importance. Negative-control and sibling-comparison designs can probe unmeasured familial and social confounding, although they introduce their own assumptions and often reduce precision. Methodological work on negative controls in epidemiology provides a framework for testing whether observed smoking-defect associations are plausibly causal rather than products of shared confounding structures ref [95], while analyses of smoking and birth outcomes using within-family contrasts illustrate both the promise and the limitations of this approach for perinatal causal inference ref [105].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Approaches in Observational Studies and Systematic Reviews
subsections.subsection_title: Meta-analytic synthesis of large observational datasets
subsections.content:
Meta-analysis of maternal smoking and birth defects is dominated by observational evidence, so synthesis must accommodate between-study differences in design, confounder control, exposure windows, and case definitions. In practice, random-effects models are often preferred because they allow the true association to vary across populations and ascertainment systems; however, when pooled datasets include very large studies, conventional inverse-variance methods can yield highly precise but still systematically biased estimates if residual confounding is shared across studies. Quantifying heterogeneity with statistics such as I² and interpreting prediction intervals are therefore more informative than focusing only on the pooled odds ratio ref [106], ref [107].

Large collaborative reviews in congenital anomaly epidemiology also face sparse-data problems for rare phenotypes, overlapping populations across registry-based reports, and differential adjustment sets. These features argue for phenotype-specific pooling rather than broad defect groupings, and for explicit sensitivity analyses separating adjusted from minimally adjusted estimates. The epidemiologic literature further emphasizes that heterogeneity should be explored substantively—through subgroup analysis or meta-regression—rather than treated solely as a nuisance parameter, especially when exposure prevalence and malformation ascertainment vary across countries and time periods ref [108], ref [109].

Methodological guidance for observational evidence synthesis additionally recommends structured assessment of study quality and cautious interpretation of small relative risks, because pooled associations may remain vulnerable to bias even when based on millions of births. Frameworks developed for meta-analysis of observational studies and for grading certainty of evidence are therefore useful complements to statistical pooling when summarizing the teratogenic literature on smoking ref [110], ref [111].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Approaches in Observational Studies and Systematic Reviews
subsections.content:
Publication bias is a persistent concern in meta-analyses of maternal smoking and congenital anomalies because the evidence base is dominated by observational studies, many of which are small, secondary analyses of birth-defect registries or case-control datasets. Positive associations for specific malformations may be preferentially published, while null findings for rare defect subtypes remain unpublished or are relegated to supplementary material. More broadly, selective outcome reporting can arise when investigators examine numerous defect categories but report only statistically notable results, inflating the apparent specificity and consistency of associations ref [112], ref [113].

Standard tools for detecting dissemination bias, such as funnel plots and Egger-type asymmetry tests, should be interpreted cautiously in this field. Congenital anomaly studies often exhibit substantial between-study heterogeneity in exposure measurement, case ascertainment, covariate adjustment, and defect classification; such heterogeneity can itself generate funnel-plot asymmetry, even in the absence of publication bias ref [114], ref [115]. The problem is magnified when outcomes are rare, because imprecise study-specific estimates and sparse-data methods can distort small-study patterns.

Accordingly, reviewers should treat publication bias assessment as a broader investigation of the reporting process rather than a single statistical test. Recommended practices include comparing published reports with protocols when available, extracting all analyzed defect categories rather than only highlighted associations, conducting sensitivity analyses restricted to large registry-based studies, and grading down certainty when selective reporting is plausible ref [113], ref [116]. In this literature, apparent replication across many nominally significant subtype analyses should therefore be weighed against the high multiplicity and selective-publication pressures inherent to observational teratology research.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Approaches in Observational Studies and Systematic Reviews
subsections.content:
Quality appraisal in reviews of maternal smoking and birth defects must move beyond generic observational-study checklists to examine design features that materially affect bias in perinatal epidemiology: prospective versus retrospective exposure capture, timing-specific smoking assessment, ascertainment of terminations and stillbirths, outcome validation, and control for major confounders such as alcohol use, socioeconomic position, maternal age, diabetes, and folate-related factors. The Newcastle–Ottawa Scale is widely used because it provides a practical framework for selection, comparability, and outcome/exposure domains, but its coarse scoring can obscure important sources of misclassification and selective case ascertainment in congenital anomaly research ref [117].

At the review level, transparent conduct and reporting are central to judging credibility. AMSTAR 2 is particularly useful because it distinguishes critical from non-critical weaknesses in systematic reviews, while the PRISMA 2020 statement improves reproducibility of search, selection, and synthesis decisions ref [118], ref [113]. For evidence grading, however, simple aggregation of statistically significant associations is inadequate. GRADE offers a structured approach for rating certainty across risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias, but observational evidence on teratogenic exposures often requires explicit consideration of residual confounding, exposure misclassification, and potential dose–response patterns before certainty can be upgraded or downgraded ref [119].

In practice, strength-of-evidence evaluation in this field is most persuasive when it triangulates several signals: consistency across study designs and eras, robustness to sensitivity analyses, biological gradient, and specificity of associations for defect subtypes rather than broad anomaly groups. This logic aligns with established causal-thinking frameworks in observational epidemiology, which emphasize that judgments should integrate magnitude, coherence, and alternative explanations rather than rely on pooled odds ratios alone ref [120].

subsections.section_title: Heterogeneity, Effect Modification, and Comparative Risk Frameworks
subsections.content:
Dose-response evidence is central to assessing whether maternal smoking contributes causally to congenital anomalies rather than merely tracking correlated social and behavioral factors. In principle, increasing cigarette consumption should strengthen teratogenic effects if fetal dose scales with intensity of exposure, but the literature has been more consistent for some outcomes than for others. A large population-based analysis of nonsyndromic orofacial clefts reported higher risks with heavier maternal smoking, supporting a graded association rather than a simple exposed/unexposed contrast ref [32]. Similar dose-related patterns have also been described in studies of gastroschisis, where heavier smoking has often been associated with larger effect estimates than light smoking ref [121].

At the same time, dose-response gradients are not uniformly linear or robust across birth-defect phenotypes. In a meta-analysis of maternal smoking and congenital heart defects, elevated risks were generally modest and heterogeneity across defect subtypes was substantial, limiting strong inference about monotonic gradients ref [122]. Measurement issues also weaken apparent dose-response patterns: self-reported cigarettes per day may not capture compensatory smoking, nicotine metabolism, or critical episodic exposure during organogenesis. Validation studies using biomarkers such as cotinine show that questionnaire-based smoking intensity can misclassify fetal dose, especially among light or intermittent smokers ref [123].

Accordingly, dose-response findings should be interpreted as supportive but not definitive evidence. Stronger gradients in certain phenotypes may indicate greater biological sensitivity or less etiologic heterogeneity, whereas null gradients may reflect exposure misclassification, threshold effects, or residual confounding rather than absence of teratogenic action. Future studies that combine repeated biomarker assessment with defect-specific analyses are more likely to clarify whether risk rises continuously, plateaus, or is concentrated at relatively low exposure levels ref [123], ref [124].

subsections.section_title: Heterogeneity, Effect Modification, and Comparative Risk Frameworks
subsections.content:
Timing is central to interpreting smoking-related teratogenicity because embryonic susceptibility is tightly linked to organogenesis. For most structural birth defects, the biologically relevant window lies in the periconceptional period and first trimester, when neural tube closure, craniofacial fusion, cardiac septation, and limb development occur. Accordingly, studies that distinguish smoking before conception, during early pregnancy, and after the first trimester generally find the strongest associations for defects arising from early morphogenesis, whereas later-pregnancy exposure is more plausibly related to fetal growth, placental dysfunction, and some functional outcomes rather than major malformations ref [125], ref [126].

This timing framework is especially clear for orofacial clefts and several cardiac phenotypes. Meta-analytic and pooled evidence has linked maternal smoking in early pregnancy with cleft lip with or without cleft palate and, less consistently, cleft palate alone, supporting a pathogenic window during weeks 4-10 of gestation ref [127]. For congenital heart defects, critical developmental windows also fall in the first 8 weeks, and epidemiologic syntheses suggest that exposure confined to early gestation may be more informative than measures averaged across the full pregnancy ref [38]. Similar reasoning has been applied to gastroschisis, where first-trimester smoking has been repeatedly implicated, although residual confounding by correlated behaviors remains a concern ref [128].

A recurring limitation is exposure misclassification: many datasets record smoking only at the first prenatal visit or as any smoking during pregnancy, obscuring quitting, reduction, or relapse across trimesters. Prospective studies with repeated assessment indicate substantial changes in smoking behavior after pregnancy recognition, meaning that nondifferential misclassification can attenuate trimester-specific effects and blur distinctions between etiologically relevant early exposure and later continuation ref [129]. Thus, timing-specific interpretation depends not only on developmental biology but also on how precisely studies capture exposure dynamics across pregnancy.

subsections.section_title: Heterogeneity, Effect Modification, and Comparative Risk Frameworks
subsections.content:
Population and geographic variation in the association between maternal smoking and birth defects likely reflects a mixture of true etiologic heterogeneity and differences in study design, exposure measurement, and background risk. Large pooled and multicenter analyses have shown that the magnitude of association is not uniform across settings, with more consistent elevations reported for some craniofacial and limb defects than for many other outcomes ref [130], ref [32]. Cross-national differences in smoking prevalence, cigarette composition, folate fortification, and prenatal screening and termination practices can all alter the observed defect spectrum and the apparent effect size.

Geographic variation may also arise because the distribution of interacting susceptibilities differs across populations. For example, evidence from case-control studies has suggested that risks associated with maternal smoking for orofacial clefts can vary by infant or maternal genotype and by nutritional context, implying that population differences in allele frequencies or diet could modify aggregate estimates ref [131]. Similar concerns apply to regional variation in socioeconomic patterning of smoking, co-exposures such as alcohol, and ascertainment through birth-defects registries versus hospital-based surveillance.

These considerations argue against treating a single summary estimate as universally transportable. Reviews and pooled analyses therefore emphasize the value of harmonized exposure definitions, registry linkage, and stratified analyses by region or population subgroup when interpreting the teratogenic literature on smoking ref [130], ref [132], ref [41].

subsections.section_title: Heterogeneity, Effect Modification, and Comparative Risk Frameworks
subsections.content:
Maternal characteristics can modify the apparent association between prenatal smoking and birth defects by shaping both biologic susceptibility and exposure measurement. Age, parity, nutritional status, body size, diabetes, and alcohol use are particularly relevant because they influence fetal development through overlapping pathways, including oxidative stress, vascular disruption, and one-carbon metabolism. In population-based analyses of smoking and orofacial clefts, effect estimates have sometimes differed across maternal age and alcohol-use strata, suggesting that smoking may act less as an isolated exposure than as part of a broader maternal risk profile ref [32], ref [133].

Nutritional and metabolic factors are especially plausible modifiers. Folate-related mechanisms have long been implicated in cleft pathogenesis, and periconceptional multivitamin or folic acid use has been associated with reduced risk of some defects, potentially attenuating risks linked to smoking-related interference with nutrient transport or methylation pathways ref [134]. Conversely, maternal obesity and pregestational diabetes are established risk factors for several structural anomalies and may amplify teratogenic susceptibility when combined with smoking, although many studies remain underpowered for formal interaction testing ref [135], ref [136].

Interpretation is further complicated by social patterning. Smoking during pregnancy clusters with lower socioeconomic position, younger maternal age, and co-exposures such as alcohol, all of which can generate residual confounding or genuine effect modification. Methodologically, this means subgroup analyses should be interpreted cautiously and, where possible, evaluated on additive as well as multiplicative scales. More refined characterization of maternal phenotype and comorbidity is therefore essential for understanding heterogeneity in smoking-related teratogenic risk ref [133], ref [136], ref [137].

subsections.section_title: Heterogeneity, Effect Modification, and Comparative Risk Frameworks
subsections.content:
Interpretation of associations between maternal smoking and birth defects must account for correlated exposures and behaviors that cluster with smoking during pregnancy. Smokers are more likely to consume alcohol, have poorer diet quality, lower folate intake, and differ in socioeconomic and prenatal care profiles, all of which may confound or amplify teratogenic risk. This clustering has been documented in large periconceptional studies, including analyses showing joint patterns of cigarette smoking and alcohol use among mothers of infants with congenital anomalies and evidence that low maternal folate intake may strengthen associations between smoking and selected defects such as orofacial clefts and cardiac malformations ref [23], ref [138].

Alcohol is especially important because it is both correlated with smoking and independently implicated in some structural anomalies. In case-control analyses of clefts and conotruncal defects, combined exposure patterns have sometimes produced higher risks than either exposure alone, although disentangling biological interaction from residual confounding remains difficult ref [139], ref [140]. Similar concerns apply to other lifestyle correlates, including illicit drug use, obesity, and micronutrient inadequacy, which are unevenly distributed across smoking strata and may influence embryonic development through oxidative stress, vascular disruption, or one-carbon metabolism.

These co-exposure structures argue for analytic strategies beyond simple covariate adjustment. Studies with detailed periconceptional exposure measurement, negative-control designs, and attention to nutritional context have been particularly informative, and they suggest that part of the apparent smoking signal may reflect broader behavioral risk profiles, while another part may represent genuine susceptibility heightened by alcohol use or low folate status ref [138], ref [141].

subsections.section_title: Heterogeneity, Effect Modification, and Comparative Risk Frameworks
subsections.subsection_title: Passive smoke and alternative nicotine exposures
subsections.content:
Evidence on environmental tobacco smoke suggests that risk may extend beyond active maternal smoking, although effect sizes are generally smaller and more difficult to estimate because exposure misclassification is substantial. Reviews of secondhand smoke in pregnancy have linked passive exposure with adverse fetal growth and other reproductive outcomes, supporting biologic plausibility for congenital effects through hypoxia, oxidative stress, and nicotine-mediated vasoconstriction, even when combustion exposure is indirect ref [142]. However, compared with active smoking, studies of birth defects and passive smoke have been fewer and often underpowered, making heterogeneity across settings especially consequential.

Alternative nicotine products complicate interpretation further. Nicotine itself crosses the placenta and can perturb embryologic pathways relevant to craniofacial, cardiac, and pulmonary development; experimental and epidemiologic syntheses therefore caution against assuming that non-combustible products are developmentally benign ref [143], ref [144]. The 2020 Surgeon General’s report similarly concluded that there is no known safe level of nicotine exposure in pregnancy and highlighted continuing uncertainty regarding long-term developmental and structural outcomes from e-cigarettes and other nicotine delivery systems ref [145].

For comparative risk frameworks, passive smoke and alternative nicotine exposures should therefore be treated neither as equivalent to combustible smoking nor as harmless substitutes. The available human evidence is most consistent with a gradient in which direct cigarette smoking confers the clearest teratogenic signal, while secondhand smoke and newer nicotine products remain plausible but less precisely quantified contributors whose impact likely depends on dose, timing, and correlated co-exposures ref [142], ref [144], ref [146].

subsections.section_title: Heterogeneity, Effect Modification, and Comparative Risk Frameworks
subsections.content:
Interpreting maternal smoking as a teratogenic exposure benefits from comparison with prenatal agents whose causal status is better established. In contrast to isotretinoin, valproate, or heavy prenatal alcohol exposure—each associated with relatively large absolute and relative increases in major structural anomalies—maternal smoking is generally characterized by smaller effect sizes that cluster around selected defect phenotypes rather than a broad malformation spectrum ref [147], ref [148], ref [149], ref [150]. This comparative framing is important because smoking may contribute materially at the population level through high prevalence even when defect-specific risks are modest.

The strongest and most consistently discussed smoking associations, such as with orofacial clefts and some cardiac defects, therefore occupy a different evidentiary and mechanistic position from classic teratogens. Meta-analytic evidence suggests elevated but moderate risks for cleft lip/palate among offspring of smokers ref [151], whereas established teratogens like valproate show substantially larger relative risks and clearer dose dependence for major congenital malformations ref [149]. Likewise, fetal alcohol exposure is linked to a wider developmental phenotype extending beyond isolated structural defects ref [150].

Thus, comparative teratogenic context helps calibrate inference: smoking should not be interpreted as equivalent in potency to canonical teratogens, yet neither should it be dismissed. Its public-health relevance derives from ubiquity, co-occurrence with other social and environmental risks, and the possibility that modest teratogenic effects interact with susceptibility factors to shift the burden of preventable birth defects.

subsections.section_title: Clinical, Preventive, and Public Health Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Implications for prenatal counseling and risk communication
subsections.content:
Prenatal counseling should communicate that smoking in pregnancy is linked not only to fetal growth restriction and preterm birth, but also to a measurable increase in the risk of selected congenital anomalies, particularly orofacial clefts and some cardiac defects. Meta-analytic evidence supports modest but consistent associations for maternal cigarette smoking with cleft lip with or without cleft palate and cleft palate alone, making these outcomes suitable for concrete, evidence-based risk communication rather than vague warnings ref [32], ref [40].

Risk communication is likely to be most effective when framed in absolute as well as relative terms, acknowledging that the baseline risk of any specific anomaly remains low while emphasizing that smoking is a preventable exposure. Counseling should also stress timing: because organogenesis occurs early, cessation before conception or immediately after pregnancy recognition is more protective than later reduction. This message is consistent with broader obstetric evidence that there is no known safe level of smoking in pregnancy and that even low-intensity smoking carries adverse perinatal risk ref [152], ref [153].

Clinicians should use nonjudgmental, trauma-informed communication that distinguishes nicotine dependence from moral failure, since stigma can reduce disclosure and engagement with care. Clear discussion of uncertainty is also important: while not every observed association is necessarily causal, the convergence of epidemiologic and biological evidence justifies precautionary advice to avoid combustible tobacco exposure entirely and to support early cessation at every prenatal contact ref [40], ref [154].

subsections.section_title: Clinical, Preventive, and Public Health Implications
subsections.content:
Smoking cessation during pregnancy is one of the few modifiable interventions with potential to reduce fetal exposure during the period of organogenesis, but effectiveness depends on both timing and treatment intensity. Behavioral support remains the cornerstone of care: counseling integrated into routine antenatal visits, motivational interviewing, and tailored self-help can increase abstinence, although effects are typically modest and relapse after delivery is common [1]. Financial incentives have shown stronger effects than many other strategies, with randomized evidence indicating substantially higher quit rates when contingent rewards are added to usual care [2].

Pharmacologic options remain more contested in pregnancy than in the general population. A large placebo-controlled trial of nicotine patches found limited sustained cessation benefit, likely reflecting poor adherence and increased nicotine metabolism in pregnancy [3]. More broadly, Cochrane synthesis suggests that psychosocial interventions improve late-pregnancy abstinence, whereas evidence for nicotine replacement therapy is less certain and must be balanced against continued smoking exposure [4]. In practice, intervention pathways should therefore prioritize early identification, repeated offers of support, partner or household smoking assessment, and postpartum relapse prevention.

Implementation should also acknowledge socioeconomic patterning of smoking in pregnancy. Women facing material deprivation, mental health comorbidity, or intimate partner stress may require more intensive, flexible, and trauma-informed cessation support rather than brief advice alone. Emerging evidence from pragmatic trials and implementation studies suggests that combining routine biochemical validation, opt-out referral systems, and incentive-based treatment can improve reach and effectiveness in maternity services [5].

subsections.section_title: Clinical, Preventive, and Public Health Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Preconception and early pregnancy prevention strategies
subsections.content:
Preconception prevention is especially important because critical windows for organogenesis often occur before pregnancy recognition, limiting the effectiveness of interventions initiated after the first prenatal visit. In practice, smoking assessment and cessation support should therefore be embedded in routine reproductive-age care, contraception counseling, and preconception visits, with explicit discussion that stopping before conception or as early as possible in the first trimester is likely to confer the greatest fetal benefit. This timing logic is reinforced by evidence that many congenital anomalies arise from developmental events in very early gestation and by public health recommendations emphasizing prepregnancy risk reduction, including tobacco avoidance, as part of preconception care ref [158], ref [159].

Effective early prevention strategies should combine universal screening for tobacco and nicotine use with rapid access to behavioral treatment, quitline referral, and follow-up tailored to pregnancy intention. Because a substantial proportion of pregnancies are unintended, population-level approaches are needed rather than relying only on pregnancy-confirmed care. Interventions should also address co-exposures that cluster with smoking and may amplify teratogenic risk, including alcohol use, poor nutrition, and inadequate folate intake; the latter remains a cornerstone of congenital anomaly prevention and is most effective when initiated before conception ref [160], ref [161].

At a policy and systems level, preconception and early pregnancy prevention can be strengthened by integrating smoking cessation into family planning services, electronic health record prompts, and pharmacist- and primary-care–led brief interventions. The rise of e-cigarette use further supports nicotine-inclusive screening and counseling, since pregnancy should not be framed as a safe context for alternative nicotine products in the absence of evidence of fetal safety. A life-course approach that links tobacco control, reproductive health, and early antenatal care is therefore more likely to reduce exposure during the period of highest embryologic susceptibility ref [162], ref [155].

subsections.section_title: Clinical, Preventive, and Public Health Implications
subsections.content:
Surveillance and registry-based monitoring are central to translating evidence on maternal smoking and congenital anomaly risk into actionable public health practice. Population-based birth defects registries, especially when linked to birth certificates, prenatal screening data, hospital discharge records, and termination-of-pregnancy data, can improve ascertainment of both exposure and outcome and support timely detection of temporal and geographic variation. Methodological guidance from established surveillance networks has emphasized the importance of standardized case definitions, active case finding where feasible, and harmonized coding to enable valid comparisons across jurisdictions ref [163], ref [164].

A recurring limitation is exposure misclassification when smoking is captured only from maternal self-report on vital records. Record-linkage studies show that smoking information on birth certificates is incomplete relative to other data sources, underscoring the value of integrating prenatal care records, questionnaire data, and, where possible, biomarker validation in sub-samples ref [165]. Surveillance systems should also distinguish combustible cigarettes from e-cigarettes, dual use, secondhand smoke exposure, timing of cessation, and smoking intensity during the periconceptional window, because etiologically relevant exposure may precede pregnancy recognition.

Registry infrastructures are also well suited for monitoring intervention impact and inequities. Large multisite collaborations such as EUROCAT and the National Birth Defects Prevention Network have demonstrated how routine data can be used to evaluate trends, identify high-risk populations, and assess policy-relevant changes in prevalence and ascertainment practices ref [164], ref [166]. Future surveillance should prioritize linkage-capable, equity-oriented systems that capture social determinants and access to cessation support, while preserving denominator quality and transparency in case ascertainment ref [163], ref [166].

subsections.section_title: Clinical, Preventive, and Public Health Implications
subsections.content:
Equity considerations are central because smoking in pregnancy is socially patterned and concentrated among women facing structural disadvantage, including poverty, low educational attainment, younger maternal age, mental health comorbidity, and social marginalization. Population-based analyses from high-income settings consistently show steep socioeconomic gradients in prenatal smoking and smoking-attributable adverse birth outcomes, implying that congenital anomaly prevention cannot rely on universal messaging alone but requires proportionate, targeted support for groups with the highest exposure burden ref [167], ref [168].
