Vulnerable populations may also face compounded risks through higher prevalence of heavy smoking, secondhand smoke exposure, unstable housing, limited access to preconception care, and lower uptake of cessation services. Indigenous populations are particularly affected in several countries, reflecting the legacy of colonization, discrimination, and unequal access to culturally safe maternity care; interventions that ignore these contexts risk widening disparities even when average cessation rates improve ref [169]. For women with mental illness or substance use disorders, nicotine dependence is often more severe and less responsive to brief counseling, underscoring the need for integrated, trauma-informed care pathways ref [170].

From a public health perspective, equity-oriented strategies should combine routine screening with enhanced referral, culturally tailored communication, financial and social support, and evaluation of intervention reach by ethnicity, deprivation, age, and geography. More complete linkage of congenital anomaly, birth, and tobacco exposure data is also needed to identify whether declines in smoking-related risk are shared equitably across populations or bypass those already at greatest disadvantage ref [171].

subsections.section_title: Clinical, Preventive, and Public Health Implications
subsections.content:
Policy responses should treat smoking in pregnancy not only as an individual behavioral risk, but also as a population exposure shaped by pricing, marketing, product regulation, and access to cessation support. Large-scale tobacco control measures—including higher excise taxes, comprehensive smoke-free laws, plain packaging, and mass-media campaigns—reduce smoking prevalence in women of reproductive age and are therefore likely to yield downstream benefits for fetal and infant health. Evidence from interrupted time-series analyses suggests that smoke-free legislation has been followed by improvements in perinatal outcomes, including reductions in preterm birth and, in some settings, stillbirth, supporting pregnancy-relevant co-benefits of broader tobacco regulation ref [172], ref [173].

Pregnancy-specific policy should be layered onto these population measures. Clinical guidelines and insurance coverage should ensure universal screening for combustible tobacco, secondhand smoke, and emerging nicotine products, with rapid access to evidence-based cessation treatment. Because financial barriers reduce treatment uptake, reimbursement for counseling and approved pharmacotherapies should be protected, while public messaging should explicitly discourage industry framing of e-cigarettes as harmless in pregnancy given major uncertainties regarding fetal safety ref [174]. Regulatory agencies should also prioritize warning labels and restrictions on youth- and pregnancy-appealing marketing claims for nicotine products.

A further implication is that tobacco control policy must be equity-oriented. Smoking in pregnancy is socially patterned, and conventional policies may have smaller effects where deprivation, stress, and unstable housing undermine quitting. Policy packages are therefore likely to be most effective when combined with targeted cessation services and, where acceptable, incentive-based approaches for disadvantaged pregnant smokers ref [19], ref [175]. At the same time, implementation should be monitored for unintended consequences such as stigma or reduced prenatal care engagement, particularly among younger women and marginalized populations.

subsections.section_title: Clinical, Preventive, and Public Health Implications
subsections.content:
Future research should move beyond conventional exposure contrasts toward designs that better address causality, timing, and dose. In particular, studies should integrate negative-control comparisons, sibling designs, genetically informed approaches, and triangulation across methods, building on the logic articulated for causal inference in epidemiology ref [176]. For smoking in pregnancy, this means distinguishing direct teratogenic effects from confounding by familial, behavioral, and socioeconomic factors, and identifying etiologically relevant windows during preconception, implantation, and early organogenesis.

A second priority is improved exposure assessment. Reliance on maternal self-report remains a major limitation, especially for intermittent smoking, secondhand exposure, nicotine replacement, and emerging products such as e-cigarettes. Prospective cohorts and registry linkages should incorporate repeated biomarker measurement and standardized anomaly phenotyping, while harmonizing core variables across surveillance systems. Existing work shows both the promise and complexity of biomarker-based assessment in pregnancy ref [177], and highlights the importance of robust congenital anomaly classification and ascertainment frameworks for epidemiologic comparability ref [164].

Future intervention research should also test whether cessation before conception or in very early pregnancy reduces anomaly risk, rather than focusing only on later obstetric outcomes. Trials and quasi-experiments should evaluate multi-component strategies, including behavioral support, financial incentives, and population-level tobacco control. Evidence that incentives can substantially improve cessation in pregnancy ref [19], together with the broad maternal-child health gains associated with comprehensive tobacco control policies ref [178], supports a research agenda that links mechanistic epidemiology with implementation and policy evaluation.
